doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

title: Playing Europe in the 1950s versus the US
summary: Long prop-plane flights, a different culture and audiences who seemed to appreciate the music more.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: What was it like playing in Europe for the most part. Was it different from the States?
It seemed so in the beginning.
Yeah, during that time, I think it was definitely different.

Well at that time, I mean the world wasn’t so accessible. Like it took us 13 hours to go over there on prop planes. We’d go up by way of Newfoundland, you know gas up up there, and then jump across the ocean on the DC-7 or what was the other, the DC-6.
DC-6. Jets hadn’t come into being.

Yeah. And the two cultures were like totally divided. Right now when you go over there you can’t feel that much different than you do in the United States. But at that point, I mean the language and everything else was just completely different. So it made us feel like we were doing something completely different ourselves, because we were hearing all the foreign languages, and we were seeing people do things differently than they do them in the United States. We couldn’t get a sandwich after about 12:00 at night. You know, it was just, it was totally different. And the women were more interesting at that point cause we were younger too. And that made a lot of difference. Don’t show this to my wife, I didn’t mean anything.

The fans seemed to appreciate the music more. I don’t know if it was actually true, but it just seemed as though larger percentages of European audiences really related to the music and back home it seemed as though lots of people would say, “well that’s all right, what else can you do?”

But over the years I’ve found that the United States has sort of caught up as far as audience appreciation of what we do, compared to the European audiences. And even in the latter years of my tour of duty with the orchestra, in the, after ‘62, ‘63, ‘64, it seemed as though when we went to Europe, we’d see whole families come to concerts, but it may just have been the father who appreciated the music and the rest of the family was just there ‘cause he brought them and maybe he wanted to expose them to this American cultural entity. And it seemed as though a lot of people came out of curiosity, “oh we’ve heard about this Count Basie Orchestra, let’s see what it’s about“ to me. Bill may have a different story, but that’s the feeling I got.
No, that’s pretty much the way I perceived it.
